explainBack.question: Why couldn't Anthropic's account bans actually stop the Mali surveillance project, even though the bans were real and complete?
explainBack.answer: Anthropic can only see and control activity on its own service. Its cross-account visibility let it find and ban every linked account — a real intervention on real evidence. But that visibility ends at its own boundary: it cannot see or block what the same actors do with other or open models. So per Axios, the Mali platform was simply rebuilt and deployed locally using other models. The ban proves the misuse happened on Claude; it does not prove the operation ended.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (visibility enables action but stops at the provider boundary), P006 (venue analogy with its stated limits), P003 (Axios: Mali system deployed locally with other models after the bans).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this causal answer: the mechanism, its limit, and the confirming real case are all explicitly present, so a reader can reconstruct the chain in ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A major email provider announces it detected and shut down 40,000 accounts run by a fraud ring that used its service to send AI-personalized phishing messages, and a headline declares 'Email giant dismantles international scam operation.'
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's evidence ladder, what did the provider actually establish, and does the headline's claim hold?
unseenTransfer.answer: The provider observed requests and an operating workflow on its own service — levels one and two of the ladder. Shutting accounts is a real intervention at that level. But 'dismantles international scam operation' asserts a real-world outcome (level four): that the ring itself is gone. The provider cannot see the ring's activity on other email services, self-hosted servers or messaging apps, so the operation may continue elsewhere — exactly as the Mali surveillance platform continued on other models. The headline over-claims; the correct claim is 'removed the operation from its platform.' A reader should ask whether any independent investigator or public authority confirmed the ring actually stopped.
